articles.title: The Vault: the numbers behind keeping your own records
articles.body: Most housing disputes come down to what can be shown, not what was said. Legal-aid organizations consistently advise tenants to keep their own dated copies of notices, letters, photos, and payment records — because a landlord's file and a tenant's memory are not the same thing. In eviction cases, a large share of tenants lose not on the merits but by missing a deadline or arriving without the document that proves their side. Semptify's answer is that the records live in the tenant's own cloud storage — Dropbox or Google Drive — not on Semptify's servers. That means the tenant keeps everything even if they stop using Semptify, and a copy of a notice or a photo can't disappear from the tenant's own account. Nothing about this guarantees an outcome; it simply means the tenant's side of the record exists, in one place, under their control.

articles.title: The Vault: what it does and how to use it
articles.body:
The Vault is the tenant's own cloud folder — a Dropbox or Google Drive account they already have or set up — where Semptify puts everything it saves for them. Semptify does not hold the files; it organizes them into folders the tenant owns.

Using it looks like this: a tenant photographs a water leak, uploads it, and the image lands in their own drive inside the vault folder. A landlord's text message saved as a screenshot goes in beside it. When the tenant later needs to show what happened and when, the files are already dated and in one place — theirs.

The practical effect: the tenant can share a folder with an advocate, download everything at any time, or stop using Semptify entirely and keep every file. The vault belongs to the tenant, not the platform.
